blocks.text: Security Architecture — Interview Prep Handout
For a Software/Solution Architect case-study interview with a VP (cybersecurity product company)
Written in English on purpose — same language as your interview, so you build vocabulary and reasoning patterns together.
1. How to use this handout
This is not a definitions dictionary — it's built around how to reason out loud in a case-study discussion. For every topic you'll find:

items: The core concept (short, no fluff)
The trade-offs a VP-level interviewer actually cares about
2–3 "thinking out loud" phrases you can reuse
A follow-up question they might throw at you

blocks.text: Read once, then talk through each section out loud in English, as if answering. That's where the real prep happens.
2. Threat Modeling & STRIDE
Core idea: before designing anything, identify what could go wrong. STRIDE is a classification of threat types:

rows: Encryption at rest/in transit, least privilege

blocks.text: Trade-off to mention: threat modeling has a cost in delivery speed — the skill is doing it proportionally (a lightweight STRIDE pass on a new service vs. a full formal review for a component handling PII/payment data).
Phrases to use:

items: "Before jumping into the design, I'd want to threat-model the data flow — who are the actors, what data crosses trust boundaries."
"The main attack surface here is X, so I'd prioritize mitigating spoofing and information disclosure first."

blocks.text: Likely follow-up: "How would you prioritize which threats to address first with limited engineering time?" → Answer using impact × likelihood, not "fix everything."
3. Zero Trust Architecture
Core idea: never trust based on network location; verify every request explicitly, every time — "never trust, always verify."
Key pillars:

items: Identity-centric: every user/service has a verifiable identity (not just "inside the VPN = trusted").
Least privilege access, granted per-request/per-session, not standing broad access.
Micro-segmentation: network split into small zones so lateral movement is limited after a breach.
Continuous verification: re-check posture/context (device health, location, behavior) not just at login.
Assume breach: design as if an attacker is already inside.

blocks.text: Trade-off to mention: Zero Trust adds latency and operational complexity (more auth checks, more policy management) — worth it for high-value systems, potentially overkill for low-risk internal tools.
Phrases to use:

items: "I'd design this assuming the network perimeter is already compromised, so authorization has to happen at every hop, not just at the edge."
"Rather than a flat VPC, I'd segment by trust zone so a compromised service can't reach everything."

blocks.text: Likely follow-up: "How does Zero Trust change how services talk to each other internally?" → mTLS between services, short-lived credentials, service identity (e.g., SPIFFE/SPIRE, IAM roles), no implicit trust from "same VPC."
4. Identity & Access — OAuth2 / OIDC / IAM
(Your strongest natural ground — you already work with AWS Cognito. Use real examples from Compass/Area Riservata here.)
OAuth2 = authorization framework (delegated access — "can this app act on my behalf"). OIDC = identity layer on top of OAuth2 (adds the ID Token — "who is this user").
Key flows to be fluent on:

items: Authorization Code + PKCE — the standard for web/mobile apps today (no implicit flow anymore — deprecated for security reasons: token leakage via browser history/redirects).
Client Credentials — service-to-service, no user involved.
Refresh tokens — short-lived access tokens + longer-lived refresh tokens, rotated on use to detect theft (refresh token rotation).

blocks.text: Access control models:

items: RBAC (role-based) — simple, coarse-grained, scales poorly with complex permission matrices.
ABAC (attribute-based) — policy evaluated on attributes (user, resource, context) — more flexible, more complex to reason about and audit.

blocks.text: Trade-off to mention: RBAC is easier to audit and explain to compliance; ABAC is more flexible for complex multi-tenant permission logic but harder to reason about at scale — many real systems use a hybrid.
Phrases to use:

items: "In my experience with Cognito-based auth, the key decision was whether to keep authorization logic centralized in the identity layer or push it down into each service — we chose..."
"I'd avoid rolling custom token validation logic and rely on a well-audited library/standard instead."

blocks.text: Likely follow-up: "How would you design authorization for a multi-tenant B2B product where each customer has different permission structures?" → this is a strong ABAC/hybrid discussion, and a great place to bring in real experience.
5. Secrets Management & Rotation
Core idea: secrets (API keys, DB credentials, certificates) must never live in code, config files, or environment variables checked into version control.
Key practices:

items: Centralized secrets store (AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault, Parameter Store).
Automatic rotation — especially for DB credentials and service-to-service tokens.
Least-privilege access to secrets themselves — not every service needs every secret.
Short-lived credentials over long-lived static ones where possible (e.g., IAM roles with temporary STS tokens instead of hardcoded AWS keys).

blocks.text: Trade-off to mention: rotation adds operational risk (a bad rotation can cause an outage) — needs to be automated and tested, not manual.
Phrases to use:

items: "I'd treat secrets rotation as a first-class operational concern, not an afterthought — tested in staging before it ever runs in prod."

blocks.text: Likely follow-up: "What happens to active sessions/connections when you rotate a credential?" → graceful rotation (both old and new valid during an overlap window) vs. hard cutover.
6. Application Security Testing — SAST / DAST / SCA
(You have real Veracode experience — lead with it.)

rows: Source code for known vulnerable patterns

blocks.text: Trade-off to mention: SAST catches issues early (cheaper to fix) but has false positives and can't catch runtime/config issues; DAST is more realistic but later in the cycle and slower. Mature pipelines use both, gated at different stages.
Phrases to use:

items: "In my current pipeline, we gate merges on SAST results through Veracode, and treat critical findings as blocking rather than advisory."
"The real challenge isn't running the scanner — it's triaging findings so real vulnerabilities aren't drowned out by noise."

blocks.text: Likely follow-up: "How do you handle a critical vulnerability found in a widely-used dependency across many services?" → SCA + centralized dependency management + a fast patch/rollout process, not manual per-repo fixes.
7. Secure Multi-Tenant Architecture
Highly likely topic for a cybersecurity product company (their whole business is protecting customer environments).
Key decisions to be ready to discuss:

items: Isolation model: shared database with tenant_id column vs. schema-per-tenant vs. database-per-tenant vs. full infrastructure isolation. Trade-off = cost/operational complexity vs. blast radius if something goes wrong.
Data residency — some enterprise/government customers require data to stay in specific regions (relevant for an "international" product company).
Noisy neighbor problem — one tenant's load shouldn't degrade another's — rate limiting, resource quotas per tenant.

Cross-tenant data leakage as the single worst failure mode — how do you prevent a query bug from ever returning another tenant's data (defense in depth: app-layer checks + DB-layer row security + tests specifically for this).

blocks.text: Phrases to use:

items: "For a security product specifically, cross-tenant isolation isn't just a bug risk — it's the core trust promise of the product, so I'd treat it as a first-class design constraint, not an implementation detail."

blocks.text: Likely follow-up: "Would you recommend shared or isolated infrastructure for a new enterprise customer with strict compliance requirements?" → depends on contract/compliance tier — good answer shows you'd tier isolation by customer segment, not use one model for everyone.
8. Compliance Frameworks — SOC 2 / ISO 27001 / GDPR
You don't need to be a compliance expert — you need to show you understand how architecture decisions map to compliance requirements.

items: SOC 2 — US-centric, trust service criteria (security, availability, confidentiality, processing integrity, privacy). Common in B2B SaaS sold to enterprise US customers. Architecturally: access logging, encryption, change management, incident response process.
ISO 27001 — international standard, broader ISMS (information security management system) — process-heavy, not just technical controls.

GDPR — EU data protection law. Architecturally relevant: data minimization, right to erasure (can you actually delete a user's data across all systems?), data residency, breach notification within 72 hours.

blocks.text: Trade-off to mention: compliance requirements sometimes conflict with product speed (e.g., "right to erasure" is hard in event-sourced/append-only systems) — good architects design for this from day one rather than retrofitting.
Phrases to use:

items: "Compliance isn't a checkbox at the end — decisions like data retention and deletion need to be designed into the data model up front."

blocks.text: 9. Cloud Security Architecture (AWS-oriented — your home turf)
Be ready to reason about, using your own stack (Cognito, Lambda, ElastiCache/Redis, OpenShift):

items: Network segmentation: VPCs, private subnets for data stores, security groups as micro-firewalls.
IAM least privilege: role-per-service, no shared broad IAM users; use of instance/task roles over static credentials.
Encryption: at rest (KMS-managed keys) and in transit (TLS everywhere, including internal service-to-service).
Logging & observability for security: CloudTrail for API-level audit, centralized log aggregation, alerting on anomalous access patterns.

Container/platform security (OpenShift/ArgoCD relevant): image scanning before deploy (ties back to SCA), signed images, least-privilege pod security policies, GitOps as an audit trail (every change is a reviewed, versioned commit).

blocks.text: Phrases to use:

items: "Because we deploy through ArgoCD, every production change is traceable to a Git commit — that GitOps trail is itself a security control, not just a delivery convenience."

blocks.text: 10. General Case-Study Reasoning Framework
When they hand you an open case ("design a system that handles X"), structure your thinking out loud like this:

items: Clarify — ask 2–3 sharp questions before designing anything (scale, compliance constraints, existing systems, what "secure" specifically means for this case).
State assumptions explicitly — "I'll assume X; let me know if that's wrong."
Identify trust boundaries and data sensitivity — what's the crown-jewel data here?
Propose a design at a high level first, then drill into the parts they push on.
Name trade-offs out loud, don't just pick one option silently — this is what a VP is actually evaluating.
Mention how you'd validate it — testing, monitoring, what would tell you it's working (or failing) in production.

blocks.text: Key English phrases for this framework:

items: "Before I design anything, I'd like to clarify a couple of assumptions."
"Let's say we assume X — I'll flag if that changes my answer."
"There's a trade-off here between Y and Z; given what you've described, I'd lean toward Y because..."
"One thing I'd want to validate post-launch is..."
"I don't have enough information to be certain — my best guess, with the caveat that I'd confirm with the security team, is..."

blocks.text: 11. Quick self-check before the interview

items: Can I explain STRIDE and Zero Trust in under 60 seconds each, in English, without notes?
Do I have 1 real story (Compass/Area Riservata or elsewhere) mapped to: IAM design, a security trade-off, and a compliance-driven decision?
Can I say the 5 "thinking out loud" phrases above without hesitating?
Do I have 2 smart questions ready for the VP about the product/security posture?

blocks.text: Good luck — this handout is meant to be talked through out loud, not just read.
